questions.prompt: A churn model is logistic regression. The weight on 'support tickets last month' is 0.4. A customer files 2 more tickets. How do their odds of churning change, other features fixed?
options: Their churn probability rises by exactly 0.8 percentage points
Their odds multiply by e^0.8, about 2.2 times higher
Their churn probability doubles because 2 x 0.4 is 0.8
Their log-odds fall by 0.8 because tickets reduce churn
questions.explanation: Each unit adds 0.4 to the log-odds, so 2 units add 0.8 and the odds multiply by e^0.8 = 2.23. The change in probability depends on where the customer starts on the sigmoid.

questions.prompt: You fit linear regression on 50 million rows with 200 features, and new data arrives every hour. Which way of fitting the weights fits best?
options: Invert X^T X directly with the normal equation every hour
Use stochastic gradient descent and keep updating as data arrives
Switch to logistic regression, which has no closed form anyway
Drop to 10 features so the normal equation stays exact
questions.explanation: Gradient methods scale to huge and streaming data and can be updated incrementally. The closed form needs all data at once, and explicitly inverting X^T X is numerically fragile.

questions.prompt: Your residual plot for a price model shows errors that grow wider as predicted price increases (a funnel). Which assumption is broken?
options: Constant error variance (homoscedasticity)
Independence between training and test sets
That the target variable is binary
That features are standardized before fitting
questions.explanation: A funnel means the error variance changes with the prediction, so the constant-variance assumption fails. A log transform of the target or robust standard errors are common fixes.

questions.prompt: A node holds 8 samples: 4 of class A and 4 of class B. A split sends all A left and all B right. What is the Gini gain?
questions.explanation: The parent has Gini 1 - (0.5^2 + 0.5^2) = 0.5 and both pure children have Gini 0, so the gain is 0.5 - 0 = 0.5.

questions.prompt: A random forest ranks 'transaction_id' as the most important feature by impurity importance. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Transaction IDs encode the fraud label, so the ranking is correct
Impurity importance favors high-cardinality features that allow many splits
Random forests always rank the first column in the data highest
The forest has too few trees for importance to be measured
questions.explanation: Impurity importance is computed on training data and rewards features with many unique values, which can split almost anywhere. Permutation importance on held-out data would expose it as noise.

questions.prompt: Your gradient boosted model's validation loss starts rising after tree 300 of 2,000 while training loss keeps falling. What should you do?
options: Add more trees so the model can recover
Increase the learning rate to converge faster
Use early stopping near tree 300, or lower the learning rate
Switch to deeper trees so each one fits more
questions.explanation: Boosting keeps reducing training error, so it overfits if run too long. Early stopping on validation loss, or a smaller learning rate with more patience, controls this.

questions.prompt: An RBF-kernel SVM gets 100% training accuracy but 70% on validation. Which change most likely helps?
options: Increase C to punish training errors harder
Decrease C and/or gamma for a smoother boundary
Remove feature scaling to keep raw units
Switch to a degree-10 polynomial kernel
questions.explanation: Large C and large gamma let the boundary wrap around individual points, which overfits. Lowering them widens the margin and smooths the boundary.

questions.prompt: A k-NN model uses income in dollars and age in years, both unscaled. What happens?
options: Age dominates because it has fewer unique values
Nothing, because k-NN is scale-invariant like trees
The model refuses to train until features are scaled
Income dominates the distance, so age is nearly ignored
questions.explanation: Euclidean distance adds squared differences, so a feature measured in thousands swamps one measured in tens. Standardizing gives both features a fair say.

questions.prompt: A Naive Bayes spam filter sees the word 'crypto', which never appeared in ham training emails. Without smoothing, what goes wrong?
options: P(crypto | ham) = 0, so any email containing it gets zero ham probability
The word is ignored, so the prediction falls back to the prior
The independence assumption makes the model crash
The filter must be retrained with a kernel to handle new words
questions.explanation: A single zero likelihood multiplies the whole product to zero, so one rare word can override all other evidence. Laplace (add-one) smoothing prevents this.

questions.prompt: Your data forms two interlocking crescent shapes plus scattered outliers. Which algorithm is the best first try?
options: k-means with k = 2
DBSCAN
PCA with 2 components
Logistic regression
questions.explanation: DBSCAN follows density, so it can trace non-convex shapes and labels sparse points as noise. k-means splits space with straight boundaries and would cut each crescent.

questions.prompt: You run k-means on 1D points 0, 1, 2, 8, 9, 10 with k = 2, starting centroids at 0 and 1. Where do the centroids end?
options: 0 and 9
1 and 9
1 and 5
questions.explanation: First pass: {0} and {1, 2, 8, 9, 10} give means 0 and 6. Next pass: {0, 1, 2} and {8, 9, 10} give means 1 and 9, which is stable.

questions.prompt: On random uniform noise with no real groups, you run k-means with k = 5. What do you get?
options: An error saying no clusters exist
One cluster, because k-means detects there is no structure
Five clusters anyway, so you must validate them
As many clusters as there are points
questions.explanation: k-means always partitions data into exactly k groups. Silhouette scores, stability checks and domain sense are needed to tell real structure from artifacts.

questions.prompt: PCA eigenvalues are 6, 3, 0.6, 0.4 (total 10). How many components keep at least 90% of the variance?
questions.explanation: Shares are 60%, 30%, 6% and 4%. The first two together keep 90%, so two components suffice.

questions.prompt: In a t-SNE plot, cluster A looks three times larger than cluster B and sits far from it. What can you safely conclude?
options: A has three times more spread than B in the original space
A and B are very different, because they are far apart
Little about size or distance; t-SNE mainly preserves local neighborhoods
A contains three times more points than B
questions.explanation: t-SNE equalizes density and distorts global distances, so cluster sizes and gaps are not reliable. Only local neighborhood structure is meaningful.

questions.prompt: You run PCA on features: height in mm, weight in kg, age in years, without scaling. What happens?
options: PC1 aligns mostly with height, the feature with the largest numeric variance
PCA scales features internally, so the result is unaffected
PC1 is always the average of all features
PCA fails because the units differ
questions.explanation: PCA maximizes variance, and a feature in millimetres has a huge numeric variance. Standardize first so each feature contributes on equal footing.

questions.prompt: Training error is 2% and validation error is 25%. Adding more data narrows the gap. What is the diagnosis and next step?
options: High bias: add model capacity
High variance: get more data or add regularization
Irreducible noise: nothing can be done
Data leakage: delete the validation set
questions.explanation: A big train-validation gap that shrinks with more data is the signature of high variance. More data, regularization or a simpler model are the standard fixes.

questions.prompt: You have 300 features, suspect most are irrelevant, and want a model that names the useful ones. Which penalty fits?
options: L2 (ridge), because it shrinks all weights evenly
No penalty, because least squares is unbiased
L1 (lasso), because it sets many weights to exactly zero
Early stopping, because it removes features automatically
questions.explanation: The L1 penalty's corners push weights exactly to zero, giving built-in feature selection. Ridge shrinks weights but almost never zeros them.

questions.prompt: You tune ridge alpha over 30 values and pick the one with the best test-set score, which you then report. What is wrong?
options: Ridge needs alpha above 1
Nothing; the test set is the most honest choice
You should have tuned on training error instead
The reported score is optimistically biased; tune on validation or CV
questions.explanation: Choosing alpha by test score turns the test set into a validation set, so the reported score overstates real performance. Keep the test set untouched until the end.

questions.prompt: You target-encode 'zip_code' using the mean churn over the whole training set, then train a model. CV accuracy is 99%, production 70%. Why?
options: Each row's own label leaked into its feature, especially for rare zip codes
Target encoding only works for ordinal categories
Zip codes should have been standardized first
Production data always has more noise
questions.explanation: Encoding computed over all rows includes each row's own label, which for rare categories nearly equals the answer. Use out-of-fold encoding with smoothing.

questions.prompt: You standardize the full dataset, then split into train and test. What problem does this create?
options: Standardization removes outliers from the test set
Test-set statistics leak into training through the mean and std
The model can no longer use categorical features
Trees can no longer split on scaled features
questions.explanation: The scaler's mean and standard deviation saw test rows, so information leaks into training. Fit transforms on training data only, ideally inside a Pipeline.

questions.prompt: Your deployed model crashes when a new product category appears that was not in training. Which fix fits a scikit-learn pipeline?
options: Drop the categorical column entirely
Retrain the model every time a request arrives
Use OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore') inside the Pipeline
Label-encode categories as consecutive integers
questions.explanation: With handle_unknown='ignore', an unseen category becomes an all-zero one-hot row instead of an error. Monitoring for new categories is still wise.
